panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of the posterior scalp of a child showing a well-demarcated but irregular patch of hair loss containing numerous broken hairs of varying lengths with regrowth, exactly matching the caption's description of trichotillomania. Trichotillomania is a configured target disease, and the presentation (irregular non-scarring patchy alopecia with broken hairs of different lengths) is the textbook classic presentation. The prior triage's 'other disease' label is incorrect because trichotillomania is explicitly listed among the configured primary disease keys.

panels.figure_caption: Patchy hair loss characterized by irregular borders and hairs in various stages of regrowth in a child with trichotillomania.
in_text_mentions: rs old, peak incidence is age 9–13 years with a strong female predominance (54, 55). Clinical presentation includes multiple non-scarring and focal patches of hair loss with irregular borders (Figure 5), little to no scale or excoriation, and presence of broken hairs of different lengths, often contralateral to the side of the body with the dominant hand (19, 56). Hair loss in trichotillomania frequently spares the occiput, as these hairs are more painful to pull out. Trichobezoars can be identified in patients who eat their pulled hairs, leading to gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Left clinical photograph (yellow circle) shows erosion of the entire scalp crown down to the skull with surrounding patchy broken-hair alopecia. Attribution to trichotillomania rests on the disease-focused article title ('Severe Trichotillomania') plus the in-text statement that the very smooth lesion borders and lesions at various stages of healing raised suspicion of self-injury and repetitive behavior. The skull-exposing erosion itself is not in the allowed vocabulary, so it is recorded as a proposed finding; the visible patchy broken-hair alopecia maps to the vocabulary finding (visual). B: Right clinical photograph (blue circle) shows another lesion, a crusted plaque behind the right ear. It is attributed to trichotillomania through the disease-focused article title together with the caption's specific manifestation ('Another lesion was noted behind the right ear') and the in-text link of the lesions to self-injury/repetitive behavior...

in_text_mentions: The initial differential diagnosis of a young type 1 diabetic with recurrent DKA, microcytic anemia, persistent granulomatous non-healing lesions, and recurrent diarrhea was broad and concerning for pyoderma gangrenosum in addition to infectious causes of ulcerative lesions, malignancy, and various forms of vasculitis. While reviewing the photographs, the very smooth borders of the lesions in addition to the lesions being at various stages of healing raised suspicion of the possibility of self-injury and repetitive behavior. Images of the skin lesions are shown in Figures 1-2.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Clinical photograph of scalp showing irregular patchy alopecia with short broken hairs, directly matching the caption's 'plaques d'alopécie, cheveux courts' and consistent with the article's severe trichotillomania. B: Clinical photograph of the frontal hairline/forehead region with sparse short hairs and eyebrow involvement, corresponding to the caption's 'sourcilles arrachés' (plucked eyebrows), a trichotillomania manifestation. C: Clinical photograph of the temporal/parietal scalp showing irregular alopecia patches with short broken hairs, matching the caption and trichotillomania. D: Clinical photograph of the dorsal hand showing excoriation scarring. The caption links it to the trichotillomania-associated excoriation behavior; scars are not a hair finding but a captioned manifestation of the same patient's condition.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Slit-lamp photograph of the right eye of an 8-year-old boy with bilateral trichotillomania; the caption and in-text describe complete loss of upper eyelid eyelashes, a human patient ophthalmic image showing the target disease. B: Slit-lamp photograph of the left eye of the same 8-year-old boy with bilateral eyelash trichotillomania; real patient image showing the target disease manifestation. C: Close-up slit-lamp view of the right upper eyelid margin of the 8-year-old boy showing loss of eyelashes, the visible manifestation of trichotillomania described in the caption. D: Close-up slit-lamp view of the left upper eyelid margin of the same patient showing loss of eyelashes, consistent with the captioned bilateral eyelash trichotillomania.

in_text_mentions: Our examination showed that there was a complete loss of eyelashes of the upper eyelid of both eyes (Figure 1). His best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 in both eyes, and his corneas were clear and did not stain with fluorescein. The anterior chamber, iris, and lens were normal. Funduscopy was within normal limits. The skin of the eyelids of both eyes were not swollen, scarred, or desquamated.
